en: *Yogāmbarasādhanopāyikā* by Amitavajra [= Vijayendrasena?].
Manuscript [C. no] NAK 3–366/vi. [S. no] bauddhadarśana 74 = NGMPP B 23/10.
Palm leaf, 12 folios [with some additional material; one folio not photographed], 32/4.5 cm.
Collated with a fragment from Matsunami 312 (old no. 230)— which appears not to have been noticed previously— and with NAK 3-366 = NGMPP A 935/3.

...for Ryugen Tanemura, for the scanning... [8] Having fashioned an image, one should then install it. [Sarnath Ed. ˆ28] Then follow the work of painting, the *bali* offering, the *piṇḍi*, and the characteristics of the *gaṇḍikā*; likewise, the consecration (*pratiṣṭhāna*) of these, as well as the taking of the renunciant vows (*pravrajyāgrahaṇa*). [9] The characteristics of the *dharmadhātus*, the planting of victory banners (*dhvajā*), the restoration of ruins (*jīrṇoddhāra*), and the removal [of images]; one should worship the *gaṇamaṇḍala*. [10] Oṃ. The *Śrīkriyāsaṃgrahakārikā* is completed.

O || This is the work of the venerable Nāgārjunapāda. On the fifth day of the dark fortnight of the second [month] of the year 28(?), it was written. This is the manuscript of Abhayagupta; it was written by him. O || By this merit, may there be well-being for the entire world. O ||
Yogāmbarasādhanabuddha [1]. [Fragment of a Yogāmbara sādhana, or perhaps a hymn. Oṃ, homage to Śrī Vajrasattva!
Having bowed with constant reverence to the Lord of Yogins, the leader of the net of yoginīs, who embodies all existence, and to the Guru, the Lord of the World, who is clothed in yoga;
In accordance with the procedure taught in the *Catuṣpīṭha*, at the request of my disciple,
that propitiation is now briefly described as a means for attaining bliss.

In this regard, the practitioner—having received initiation according to the procedure taught in the *Catuṣpīṭhatantra*, being devoted to the guru, having faith in the profound Dharma, adorned with the ornaments of yoga, and seated on a comfortable seat in a place conducive to the mind such as a monastery or a grove—should perform the propitiation of the Yogāmbara who resides in the center of the maṇḍala-circle.

Therein, first of all, having visualized a red syllable *Aṃ* on the palm of the right hand, one should meditate upon a five-pronged vajra produced from the seed-syllables *Suṃ*, *Kṣuṃ*, *Yuṃ*, *Huṃ*, and *Aḥ* on the fingers of the white and other [colored] hands in sequence. Likewise, on the palm of the left hand, one should visualize the syllable *Saṃ* within a lunar disc; from that very seed-syllable, produced by the seeds of yellow orpiment (*rocanā*) and so forth, one should meditate upon a lotus. This is the procedure for purifying the hands.

Then, at the throat, an eight-petaled lotus is formed by the syllable *hrīḥ*; on the petal of the tongue-lotus, a vajra is formed by the syllable *hūṃ*. In its center is the mantra: *oṃ aḥ jihvāsaṃvartini hūṃ phaṭ*. This is the procedure for purifying the tongue.

Then, having joined the white [syllable] upon the rays of the sun with gnosis, consisting of the arrangement of the eight limbs: *kṣūṃ* on the head; *huṃ* on the two eyes; *yuṃ* on the ears and nose; *suṃ* on the tongue; *smryuṃ* on the throat; *hmryuṃ* on the two arms; *ymryuṃ* on the heart; *kṣmryuṃ* on the navel. *Oṃ vajrakāya hoḥ*: the empowerment of the body.
*Oṃ vajravākye aḥ*: the empowerment of speech.
Oṃ vajracitte hūṃ. This is the consecration of the mind (*cittādhiṣṭhāna*).

Following that, [one prepares] the conch shell and other vessels for the *argha* and *pādya* offerings. With this mantra, accompanied by the appropriate mudrā, one should empower [the offerings] twenty-one times—three sets of seven—and then set them out. As for the mudrā for this, it is the *vajrabandha*, with the three impurities raised like smoke.

In the same manner, having formed the *vajramuṣṭi* mudrā and empowered it with white collyrium (*śvetāñjana*), one should consecrate it with the *mudrā* of the gracefully tossed lotus, conch, and smoke, and recite the mantra: "Oṃ, accept this excellent honor! Svāhā! Having thus consecrated it, one should set out the water for washing the feet (*pādya*). This is the ritual procedure for the *pādya*.

Furthermore, the vessel for the offerings should be consecrated by reciting the mantra together with the *siṃhinī-mudrā* and then set aside. The mantra is: *oṃ sarvasaṃśodhani hūṃ phaṭ*. This should be recited twenty-one times, three sets of seven. This is the procedure for sprinkling the components of the worship.
Then, one should perform the protection of oneself, the removal of obstacles, and the construction of the stakes, the cage, the fence, and so forth, in this sequence: first,
having extended the moon and the sun, encircled by primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) and discernment (*vijñāna*),
one should form the shape of a swan’s wing, rotate it, and place it at the heart.
With this mudrā, accompanied by the mantra *oṃ hūṃ phaṭ*, one should armor oneself; this is self-protection (*ātmarakṣā*). Then:

upon a moon produced from the sun and moon, with smoke rising from the three impurities, one should perform the binding of the directions, the ritual pegs, the cage, the enclosure, the maṇḍala, and so forth, using this mudrā joined with the sound of the syllable *hūṃ* and through its symbolic gestures (*abhinaya*).
Having formed two vajra-fists and raised the white *ārocanā* [ointment],
one should kiss the tips of those two; then, having raised the *dhūmātra* and *malam*, one should consecrate [the disciple] with this [mudrā] upon the head,
above the forehead, on the back of the head, or above the left ear.

One should visualize Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi, colored white, blue, yellow, red, and green respectively, abiding in the mudrās of the *bodhyagrī* (enlightenment-topknot), earth-touching, boon-granting, supreme meditative concentration, and protection from fear, beautifully adorned with all ornaments and garments.
The mantra is: OṂ HŪṂ AḤ SVĀHĀ.
Having formed two vajra-fists, one should raise the white *arocana* [pigment].
One should armor the two [shoulders], the crown of the head, the heart, and the back with this mantra:

*oṃ ṭa ṭu hūṃ svāhā*. Having encircled [the body] three times with this mantra, *oṃ hūṃ svāhā*, one should satisfy [the deity] with the *samatāla* gesture while reciting *oṃ vajra tuṣya hoḥ*. Then, seated in the sattvaparyaṅka posture with the gaze fixed on the tip of the nose, one should visualize the maṇḍala adorned with the body of the deity possessing the characteristics to be described below, and worship it with perfumes and other offerings. In this regard, the following are the mudrās and mantras.

First, extending the "sun-hand" (the right hand), one should employ the fragrance mudrā: *oṃ hūṃ svāhā*. This is the mantra of the fragrance mudrā. Having joined the white [hand] with wisdom (the left), one should visualize the flower mudrā: *oṃ suṃ svāhā*. This is the mantra of the flower mudrā.
Then, contracting the conch and lotus [hands], one should employ the incense mudrā: *oṃ aḥ svāhā*. This is the mantra of the incense mudrā.
With the Sūryavajra fist, the thumb is raised. Oṃ kṣuṃ svāhā. This is the mantra of the lamp mudrā.
With the right hand extended like the sun and moon and the thumb raised: *oṃ īṃ svāhā* | *oṃ sthaṃ svāhā*. This is the offering of the *nivedya-bali*.

Then, having performed the *kamalāvarta* gesture and placed the *vajrāñjali* at the heart, one should prostrate with the five-fold maṇḍala using this [mantra]: *oṃ namas te hūṃ namāmi* | *hūṃ namo nama hūṃ svāhā*.
One should again perform the prostration three times with these mantras.
Oṃ, I offer myself for the service and worship of the five ḍākinīs. Oṃ, I offer myself for the service and worship of the preceptor.
Oṃ, I offer myself for the protection of all sentient beings.
You are the commitment; *samaya* ho 3!
Then one should perform the taking of refuge in the Three Jewels and so forth:
"I go for refuge forever to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."
For Ḍākinī is the secret of yoga and so forth for all those of the three vehicles.
I go for refuge forever, especially to the great-souled Bodhisattvas, the heroes, the heroines, and the goddesses, as well as to the Ācārya.
May all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, headed by Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Ratnāgrya, Lokeśa, and Amoghasiddhi, attend to me!
I, [name], from this moment until I sit at the seat of enlightenment, generate the supreme, unsurpassed mind of awakening.
Just as the Protectors of the three times have made their resolve for perfect enlightenment,
so too [should one practice] the threefold training in ethical discipline and the gathering of wholesome qualities.
I firmly undertake the ethical discipline of acting for the benefit of sentient beings.
From this day forward, I shall uphold the supreme and unsurpassed Three Jewels— the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha— and the vow born of the yoga of the Buddha.
I shall truly receive the vajra, the bell, and the mudrā.
And I shall accept a master within the exalted assembly of the Great Vajra Family.
I shall bestow the fourfold gift six times every day,
during the auspicious and delightful occasion of the Great Jewel Family.
I receive the True Dharma— outer, secret, and belonging to the three vehicles—
within the pure Mahāpadma family, which gives birth to great awakening.
I truly undertake the vow associated with all [deities] in the exalted assembly of the Mahākarmakula, performing the rite of worship according to my ability.
Having generated the supreme, unsurpassed mind of awakening,
and having undertaken the complete vow for the sake of all sentient beings,
I shall ferry across those who have not crossed over, and I shall liberate those who are not liberated.
"I shall bring comfort to beings who have not yet found comfort; I shall establish them in final liberation."

Then, established in the mudrā of meditative concentration with the gaze fixed on the tip of the nose, one should visualize the syllable *kṣuṃ* at one’s own heart, garlanded with rays of light and consisting of the burning away of the body. Having rendered the entire world-system devoid of appearance until only the seed-syllable remains, one should recite the mantra: *oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ svabhāvaśuddho ’ham*, and resolve upon the selflessness of all phenomena (*sarvadharmanairātmya*).

Then, one should visualize oneself being exhorted by the four goddesses, Vajraḍākinī and the others, in order to generate the *dharmasaṃbhogakāya*, which is the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the *dharmakāya*. With this [mantra]:
"Ja ja ja ja Vajrasattva! O Lord who possesses the perfection of descent, ha ha ha ha hūṃ! I am the pledge (*samaya*); I bow to you."
*Va va va va vajrastho vajraguhyodgatadehadhara!

A a a a a aho toṣya vajra alimekasulīpana hūṃ!* Then, having visualized the form of a moon mandala, one should say: "I am Jñāna. Furthermore, one should visualize above that a full moon mandala perfected by the letters beginning with *A*. Within its center, one should contemplate the syllable *HŪṂ*, which transforms into a vajra with the seed-syllable situated in the hub (*varaṭaka*). Reciting the excellent mantra, one should cultivate the divine pride (*ahaṃkāra*).
Oṃ, all phenomena are vajra-pure; I am vajra-pure.

Then, having emanated the forms of all Tathāgatas produced from radiating vajra-rays, and having performed the welfare of all sentient beings in all world-systems, one should withdraw them again and cause them to enter back into that very place, and assume the pride of the mantra: Oṃ, I am the present Hūṃ! Hūṃ! Iṭi.
Then, [one should visualize him] as complete with all the marks, solely intent on the welfare of sentient beings,
having three faces and six arms, with a luster like that of a dense rain-cloud,
possessing three eyes, smiling yet wrathful, and endowed with the sentiment of erotic passion (*śṛṅgārarasa*).
Seated in the sattvaparyaṅka posture, he is distinguished by a crown of skulls.

One should meditate upon oneself as the Lord, the sky-like expanse of the union with the Buddhas, whose body blazes with the rays of a Victor, who is embraced by the limb of Wisdom, and who bears a vajra, a thunderbolt, a bell, a vessel, and a bow.
Then, maintaining the ego-identity (*ahaṃkāra*) of Yogāmbara, one should recite this mantra:
*oṃ udbhavo haṃ | a ā ā āṃ hūṃ svāhā*.
In this way, one should contemplate [himself] as established in the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*).
"Oṃ, all phenomena are pure through yoga; I am pure through yoga.
While brandishing the vajra, one should recollect this mantra:
"Oṃ, I am the body of gnosis."
Then, with one's own samaya-mudrā accompanied by the mantra, one should empower the heart, throat, and crown.
Having joined the lotus with gnosis, the earth-parasol is joined with primordial wisdom.
Having bound the chain with two [fingers], one should form the remaining banner.
Vajradhṛk holds the smoke-bannered trident of the three impurities and the five-pronged [vajra].

"Oṃ, I am the pledge, hūṃ hūṃ; you are the pledge, empower me!"—this is the mantra. Then, having reflected, "I shall act for the benefit of sentient beings by means of the construction of the maṇḍala," one should bring it forth.
This is the samādhi called "Initial Application."

Having visualized, in due order, the mandalas of wind, fire, water, and earth, as well as the ocean, and having visualized in their center the syllables *hūṃ suṃ hūṃ* representing Great Mount Meru composed of the seven precious gems; then, with the mantra *oṃ hūṃ svāhā*, one should empower the ground as being made of vajra by means of the upturned hand. With that same mantra, upon the summit of Meru, one should visualize the maṇḍala of the Yogāmbara, situated within a peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) made of the seven precious gems, which is square, possesses four doors, and is adorned with four archways (*toraṇa*).
Abundant with dangling necklaces and half-necklaces, adorned with a network of tinkling bells;
beautified by a triple-line [pediment] and banners marked with the lion, the peacock, the royal swan, and the fish;
and graced at the corners of its four necklaces by the moon and the thunderbolt.

There, in the inner enclosure, one should place the seats of the lion, elephant, peacock, garuḍa, and kiṃkara in the four cardinal directions, and likewise in the intermediate directions starting from the northeast, the seats of the lion, the vajra-beaked [bird], the buffalo, and the jackal; thus one should preside over the nine compartments. And at the four gates, there is the seat of the corpse.
Beyond that, it is established with a garland of vajras.
Beyond that is a circular wheel. In the place of all the deities, there is the foundation of a moon and lotus.

Then, having instantly visualized a moon and lotus seat upon the outer rim-band, one descends from the sky and should contemplate the Buddha-Yogāmbara seated upon a lion throne as before, by means of the mantra.

Then, having emanated Vajraḍākinī from the heart with the syllable *suṃ*, and having established all sentient beings—according to their individual capacities—in everything from the generation of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) to taking refuge in the Three Jewels, she returns by means of the yoga of withdrawal. One should visualize oneself as Vajraḍākinī, white in color, seated upon an elephant in front [of the central deity], with two arms, holding a *khaṭvāṅga* and a yogic bowl (*yogapātra*), three-eyed, with disheveled hair, wearing a crown of Buddhas, sounding the syllable *hūṃ*, clad in an elephant hide, draped in human skin, seated upon an elephant atop a sun disk, and assuming a graceful, languid posture. "Suṃ! I am Vajraḍākinī."

In the same way, having emanated the terrible Ḍākinī by means of the syllable *KṢŪM*, one should contemplate oneself as that terrible Ḍākinī—golden in color, with a terrifying loud laugh, hair standing on end, wearing a crown of the five Buddhas, seated in the half-lotus posture upon a peacock throne in the north, adorned with ornaments of snakes, holding a *khaṭvāṅga* and a yogic bowl in her hands, standing within a mandala of fire, and dressed in the same garments and cloak as Vajraḍākinī—having thus made all sentient beings blinded by ignorance possessors of the divine eye, and having returned again through the yoga of withdrawal. [One recites: "I am the syllable *KṢŪM*, the terrible Ḍākinī."

In the same way, having emanated "Yūṃ Vettālaḍākinī" and filled the entire expanse of space with the form of Vettālī, and having established all sentient beings on the path to enlightenment, one returns and becomes a single mass. One should then visualize Vaitālaḍākinī in the western direction, seated upon a Garuḍa throne in the utkaṭa posture, crimson like coral, and otherwise resembling Vajraḍākinī, abiding in the form of Vettālī. One should cultivate the ego-identification: "Yūṃ Vettālī, I am [she]."

In the same way, having uttered "Hūṃ! I am Caṇḍālī," through the yoga of radiating from the heart and fulfilling the desired aims of all sentient beings as they wish, one returns and becomes Caṇḍālī in a singular form. One should assume the ego-identity with "Hūṃ! I am Caṇḍālī," appearing as she was manifested and emerged, standing poised, blue in color with disheveled red hair, seated in the paryaṅka posture reaching down to the knees, with palms joined at her head, and otherwise resembling a terrible ḍākinī. Likewise, one should visualize Siṃhinī, white and yellow in color, wearing red garments, and possessing two arms.

One should visualize Siṃhinī, who burns all Māras; she holds a sword aloft in her right hand and a noose with the index finger in her left. One should contemplate her seated in the *lalitākṣepa* posture upon a lion throne in the northeast.

Likewise, in the southeast, one should visualize a tigress produced from the seed-syllable *hmryuṃ*, white-black in color and wearing red garments, with two arms holding a goad in the right hand and a noose in the left. She is seated upon the previously mentioned seat by means of the casting of the mandala. In the southwest, one should visualize a jackal-faced female jackal produced from the seed-syllable *ymryuṃ*, red-black in color and wearing red garments, with two arms holding an axe and a noose, seated in the half-lotus posture upon the previously mentioned seat.

In the northwest, one should visualize [the goddess] born from the seed-syllable *kṣmryuṃ*, having the face of an owl, red-yellow in color, two-armed, holding a staff and a noose, and seated in the utkuṭuka posture upon the previously prepared seat.

In the four gates starting from the east, having sequentially established upon the previously prepared corpse-seats those generated from the seed-syllables PHŪṂ (Ḍākinī), PHEṂ (Dīpinī), PHOṂ (Cūṣiṇī), and FRĪṂ (Kāmbojī)—who are white, yellow, red, and black in color, respectively; who have their hands cast into their mouths with the palms joined above the head like a lamp; who hold handfuls of blood to their mouths and raise clubs with their two arms from their hearts; and whose hair is disheveled—one should emanate these gatekeepers, Ḍākinī and the others, from one's heart and establish them in the inner wheel, outside the vajra-fence.
In the east are Pokkasī, Drāmiḍī, and Caṇḍī, produced from the seed-syllables *ha*, *ho*, and *hrīḥ*; their three hands are occupied holding vessels of nectar and radiance.
In the north are Ghorī, Rudhirā, and Māṃsī, born from the seed-syllables *ghrīṃ* and *ghuḥ*; they hold five goads, full lotuses, and vessels.
In the west are Ugrī, Jvalitā, and Bhībhatsī, transformed from the seed-syllable *kuru-kuru*, each holding a vessel of offerings in her hand.
The three—Kapālī, Vajrī, and Kumbhī—transformed from the three seed-syllables of the *vatuli*, hold vessels for food and drink in their right hands.

In the four corners beginning with the northeast: *Hūṃ Lāsyā*. *Supriya Gandhe Hūṃ*: Lāsyā arises from the seed-syllable, holding a *garva* mudrā in one hand and busy with a vessel of perfume in the other. Thus, Lāsyā and Gandhā [are established]. In the southeast: *Hūṃ Ho Śrīṃ*. Vīṇā. Puṣpā. [These two] delight in the offering of playing the lute and scattering flowers.

In the southwest, [is] Gītā, born from the seed-syllables HŪṂ and ĪṂ; she holds incense before her face, which is white due to its movement, and her hands are occupied with an incense burner. In the northwest, [is] Sunṛtyā, born from the seed-syllables HŪṂ and KṢUṂ; she stands dancing with her hands joined above her head, occupied with a lamp. These are Nṛtyā and Dīpā. All of these should be visualized as adorned with fragrant and variegated flower garlands.
In the middle mandala is a circular wheel.
Then, at the eastern gate of the outer mandala, one should worship Hari with "Khe Saḥ";
at the northern gate, Brahmā with "Oṃ";
and at the western gate, Maheśvara with "Hūṃ Saḥ."
At the southern gate, one should worship Śakra with the mantra "mu mu";
in the northeast, Indra with "su mu";
and in the southeast, Kubera with the mantra "dhanāgri."
In the southwest, one should worship Bhūtarāja with the mantra "khātani";
in the northwest, Varuṇa with the mantra "bhūr bhuvaḥ";
and on the panel of deities, starting from the east.
Oṃ kūṃ a svāhā! Karaṅkabhairava. Oṃ khūṃ ā svāhā! Khaṭvāṅgarākṣasa. Oṃ gūṃ i svāhā! Gaṇeśvara.
Oṃ ghūṃ ī svāhā. Ghaṇṭākarṇa.
These are the colors of the ḍākinīs on the northern band.
Oṃ cūṃ u svāhā | Caṇḍeśvara.
Oṃ chūṃ ū svāhā | Chandodeva. Oṃ jūṃ ṛ svāhā | Jvareśvara.
Oṃ jhūṃ ṛ svāhā. Jhaṅkārabhīṣaṇa. These are the syllables of the Dīpinī. Pa.
[7] Rocanaśṛṅkhalā: Oṃ smryuṃ svāhā. Siṃhī.
Having firmly bound its mudrā, [one recites] "Oṃ hrmryuṃ svāhā" when the three impurities have risen like smoke. This is Vyāghrī.
Having firmly bound his mudrā, he formed the earth-umbrella and the lotus-chain.
Oṃ ymryuṃ svāhā | Jaṃbukī!
By those who have bound the two vajra-bands and extended them against one another, [the fetters are released].
Oṃ kṣmryuṃ svāhā | Ulūkī | This is the heart-mantra for the nine goddesses beginning with Garbhā, together with their mudrās.

Outside the Vajra-fence, one should employ the deity-mantra together with its mudrā; having extended the hand like a moon, it is joined by the "breaking" gesture (*bhaṅgavijñā*). With two [fingers] at the front, one should kiss [it], preceded by nectar-water.
Oṃ ha ho hrīḥ svāhā!
Pūrvayoginī!
Having extended the moon-hand, [form] a hollowed cup (sampuṭa) over the sun.
Oṃ ghriṃ ghra svāhā. This is the Northern Yoginī.
Having firmly formed the vajrāñjali mudrā, one should cause the moon and sun to scatter.
Oṃ kuru 2 svāhā!
[This is] the western yoginī.
Having extended the moon and sun, the back is joined with the back.
To the right of the cumba that has been rotated at the front, there is the Dakṣiṇa-yoginī with three [syllables]:
Oṃ vatuli 2 hūṃ svāhā. This is the Dakṣiṇa-yoginī.
Having formed two vajra-fists, one should place them at the two hip joints.
Oṃ hūṃ svāhā. This is Lāsyā.

Extending the moon-hand (the left hand) and knowing its breaking [gesture], one should grasp the raised sun (the right hand) with the entire [hand] in the conch-mudrā, fragrant as it were. Oṃ supriyagandhe hūṃ.
The fragrance mudrā:
[forming] a lute with the hands,
[recite] OṂ HŪṂ HO SVĀHĀ.
Forming a hollowed cup with both hands in the añjali gesture, one should cast [the offering] upward while revolving it.
Oṃ śrīṃ svāhā. Flower.
In the southeast: having formed a fist and raised it white [in color], it is moved at the tip of the mouth.
Oṃ hūṃ 3 svāhā.
Gītā: Having firmly formed the vajramuṣṭi mudrā, the joint is grasped by the moon. Oṃ i svāhā.
In the southwest: Dhūpā.
Having firmly formed the *sūryamuṣṭi* mudrā, one should cast the *jñāna* upward.
Oṃ kṣuṃ svāhā.

One should place Dīpā at the junction of the right hip; one should place Candrapāṇi at the junction of the left arm and shoulder, and having placed Sūrya at the junction of the right arm and shoulder.
Oṃ sunṛtye hūṃ svāhā!
[The goddess] Nṛtyā is in the northwest.
Having cast the moon and sun into her mouth, she laughs.
Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ svāhā | Ḍākinī | Placing [the hands] in añjali upon the head.
Oṃ phuṃ phrāṃ svāhā;
Dīpinī is in the north.
Having cast the *añjali* of the *preta*s into his mouth.
Oṃ pheṃ phraṃ svāhā!
Cūṣiṇī is in the west.
Having firmly formed the vajra-fist, one should apply it to the root of the ear.
Oṃ phriṃ phuṃ svāhā.
Kambojī is on the right.
All [the goddesses] individually should be joined to the heart-mantra of the triple-seal (trimudra).
One should display the Vajrasphoṭa [mudrā], which belongs to all the yoginīs and deities.
Having formed two vajra-fists, one should join them back-to-back.
Oṃ vajrasphoṭa vaṃ.
The mantra for the Vajrasphoṭa mudrā: Drawing back the arrow to the edge of the ear, moving it to the heart— Oṃ Kṣūṃ Svāhā.
Seizing with an arrow;
embracing and grasping her breasts with both hands:
*oṃ priyatame hūṃ*.
Grasping the breasts, one should extend the solar portion and join it with the white gnosis;
having raised that smoke, the vajra-mudrā is displayed.
Oṃ hūṃ svāhā | Vajraṃ | The bell-mudrā is proclaimed as that which should be joined with that moon.
The bell, the joined palms, the sun and moon, the lotus, the ground, the parasol, and the moving [gesture];
these should be applied to the secret place, and they are proclaimed as the bee-seal (alimudrā).
Oṃ aḥ svāhā!
Having made a fist, one should throw it upward.
Oṃ khe sa svāhā!
Having first formed the "Hari-fist" (hari-muṣṭi), one should move it to the location of the heart. Oṃ oṃ svāhā.
In the north, Brahmā;
one should raise a triple-bannered flag upwards.
Oṃ hūṃ saḥ svāhā.
In the west is Rudra. Having raised the Rocanā [mudrā], one should extend the Sūryahasta [mudrā] and apply it at its very tip.
Oṃ mu mu svāhā.
On the right is Chatradhara.
Having formed a fist at the forehead, one should likewise touch it with the white Dhūmā.
Oṃ mu mu svāhā. In the northeast is Śakra. Having relied upon both [hands], one raises white *arocana* with the two fists.
At the front, a jewel-shaped [seal] is joined to the kissed-kisser;
*oṃ dhanāgre hūṃ svāhā*.
In the southeast is Kubera.
Forming a fist with the white [hand] raised:
Oṃ sātani hūṃ phaṭ!
In the southwest is the Lord of Beings (bhūtādhipati).
Having formed a fist, [one offers] white smoke rising upwards:
*oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svāhā*.
In the northwest is Varuṇa.
Having formed two vajra-fists, with the three impurities raised as smoke,
she who kisses the tip from the front is proclaimed as Sattvavajrī.
One should apply the general mudrā for Karaṅka, Bhairava, and the others.
"Mantra" means that one's own respective mantra is to be understood; namely:
Oṃ hūṃ a svāhā. Karaṅkabhairava.
Oṃ khūṃ ā svāhā | Khaṭvāṅgarākṣasa! Oṃ gūṃ i svāhā |
The Leader of the Gaṇas: Oṃ ghūṃ ī svāhā.
Ghaṇṭākaṇṭha.
Oṃ cūṃ u svāhā | Caṇḍeśvara | Oṃ chūṃ ū svāhā |
Cchikkanāda: Oṃ jūṃ ṛ svāhā. Jvareśvara.
Oṃ jhūṃ ṛ svāhā | Jhaṣakrodha.
Oṃ ṭūṃ ḷ svāhā |
Ṭoṇḍabhairava: Oṃ ṭhūṃ Ḷ svāhā. Ṭhaṇḍilakrodha.
Oṃ ḍūṃ e svāhā | Ḍamaruḍambara | Īṃ ḍhūṃ ai svāhā |
Ḍhakkanāda: Oṃ tūṃ o svāhā. Tumbureśvara.
Oṃ thūṃ au svāhā | This is the Thora-nāda. Oṃ dūṃ aṃ svāhā |
Daṇḍakrodha: Oṃ dhūṃ aḥ svāhā. Dhanadakrodha.
These are their pledge-seals (samayamudrā).
As for the Dharma-mudrā: one should visualize a vajra upon the lotus-petal of one’s own tongue, and in its center, one’s own mantra, the syllable of Dharma;
this becomes the Dharma-mudrā.
The Karma-mudrā is as before.
Having visualized a universal vajra at the heart of one’s own deity with the syllable *suṃ*, there is the action seal (*karmamudrā*) devoid of signs.
In this very context, the great seals (*mahāmudrā*) of all deities, such as Yogāmbara and others, consist of those endowed with signs.

Then, having worshipped the deities of the Yogāmbara maṇḍala with the eightfold worship beginning with *lāsya*, [one offers] smoke, which is free from the three stains and raised high, into the hand consisting of sun and moon. With this, the offering water: *oṃ pratīccha arghaṃ hūṃ svāhā*.
Having worshipped again with flowers and so forth, [recite]: *oṃ pravarasatkāraṃ pratīccha svāhā*.
Then, having worshipped as before with perfumes and other offerings, one should worship according to this sequence with the twenty-fold worship.
In that regard, these are the twenty: for each, preceded by the *kamalāvarta*, there are *lāsya* and the others.
Lutes, flutes; drums, small kettledrums; fans; banners, canopies; flags; parasols; musical instruments;
girdles of muñja grass; drums; dances; laughter; and the erotic sentiment.

Wrath; drawing out the arrow; raising the vajra; pressing the breasts; and with the gesture of the añjali—thus [one should act]. In all cases, however, one should employ the syllable *hūṃ* as the mantra.
Then, having held the vajra according to its true nature (*tattva*), one should ring the bell according to the Dharma (*dharma*).
Oṃ vajraghaṇṭe raṇita praraṇita saṃpraraṇita sarvabuddhakṣetrapracālite prajñāpāramitānādasvabhāve hūṃ 3 hoḥ. One should perform the praise with these and similar verses.
Possessing three faces displaying the sentiments of the erotic, the wrathful, and the laughing, with three eyes,
their bodies are as intensely beautiful as the luster of a great sapphire.

With six arms marked by the six auspicious signs, holding a khaṭvāṅga, a vessel, a sword, a flaying knife, a vajra, and a bell, he cuts through the turmoil of the hells with cries of "Hā! Hā! and laughter.
O bestower of liberation, who transcends the world through the realization of existence;
you, whose pair of feet is saluted by Jñānaḍākinī.

The embodiment of the glorious body, bearing the color that pacifies all evils; holding a khaṭvāṅga, a boon-granting mudrā, and a skull-cup; the destroyer of the afflictions within the great ocean of the sea of saṃsāra.
You are the one whose pair of feet is saluted by the Vajra-Ḍākinīs.
Śrī Ratnamūrti, whose body is of most enchanting complexion,
holding a khaṭvāṅga and a vessel filled with supreme nectar,
causes the bodies of many suffering sentient beings to swell.
O terrible Ḍākinī, whose pair of feet is saluted by all!
Possessing the excellent form of the glorious Dharmamūrti like a beautiful ruby,
holding a khaṭvāṅga staff aloft and a vessel for the fierce sentiments and so forth,
he is the one who severs the bonds of worldly existence for all beings.
He whose pair of feet is saluted by Vetālas and Ḍākinīs.
Śrī Karmamūrti possesses a most terrible form with a greenish hue;
he wields a fierce khaṭvāṅga staff and holds a human skull filled with flesh and blood,
acting as the severer of the bonds of existence arising from the afflictions such as passion.
Her pair of feet are saluted by the Caṇḍāla-Ḍākinīs.
To Śrī Siṃhī, Vyāghrī, Varāhī, Jambukī, and Lūkinī—
who hold the threatening gesture, the noose, the auspicious goad, and the axe—
and who cause the separation of all [enemies] through manifold sufferings of parting.
O you who possess a form of illusion, homage be to your pair of feet!
You are the Ḍākinī, the excellent Dīpinī, Cūṣiṇī, and Kambojinī; you are the fierce Ugranīṣu, the protectress of the world, and the destroyer of the wicked spells of evil adversaries.
Having prostrated before everything, [he bowed] at the pair of feet of the goddess Ḍākinī.
The graceful dance of the mind, enchanting and composed of thought;
the song of beautiful words accompanied by the resonance of music; the exquisite dancing of lovely women; and the finest incense made from various, most wonderful flowers.
Having beheld the fragrance of the auspicious lamp of knowledge.
The wheel of the yoga of the supreme secret consort Vīryendrā;
the yoga, the ultra-yoga, the subsequent yoga, and the great good yoga;
always exerting effort with devotion toward the speech of the True Body (satkāya).
I bow to the one who has performed the supreme worship of the venerable Śrī Guhyapīṭha.
The reality of the one who wears the crest-jewel of the play of the venerable Tattvarājaparameśvara,
whose body is radiant with the supreme beauty of the venerable Guhyapīṭha,
and who possesses the resonance and movement of the venerable vajra-bell.
The enjoyment and experience of the supreme lordship of the glorious attainment of knowledge.
Having thus performed the praise, one should ring the bell.
Oṃ śuddhadharme hūṃ aṃ ā ā āṃ svāhā! By this much, one should meditate on the nature of the selflessness of all phenomena, from the four yogas up to the great yoga,
until weariness arises.
If there is weariness, as before, one should worship with all offerings and the like, and cause the *bali* to be given.
Then, having constructed the mandala in this sequence, one should first invoke [the deities] in front.
Having formed two vajra-fists, one should join them back-to-back.
The earth-canopy of the lotus-enclosure is raised with white *arocana* pigment;
the supreme deity-attracting [mudrā] of the white-curved attractor is the pledge-mudrā (*samayamudrā*).
Oṃ vattali mahāvattali hūṃ 3 jaḥ svāhā. This is the invocation mantra (*āvāhanamantra*).

Then, having offered the water for the guest-offering (*argha*) and the water for sipping (*ācamana*), one should take the vessel of the sacrificial offering (*balibhāṇḍa*)—which contains perfumes, flowers, incense, and whatever else is available according to one's means, along with the five nectars, the hook, and the food offerings such as *jambūhika*—and, touching it with the hand while reciting the mantra beginning with "ekavṛkṣe," one should present it.
Oṃ! Whether at a solitary tree, in a cremation ground, on a mountain, in a cave, or a grotto;
by the side of a village, on a path, in a field, or especially in an empty house.
When the vessel is placed upon the ground, one should especially worship Mātaṅga;
[one should worship] Kṛṣṇarudra, Mahārudra, and that which is supported by Devadatta;
[and] Kṛṣṇa, Karāla, Bhībhatsa, Nandātīta, and Vināyaka.
Cāmuṇḍī is the terrible and loathsome one, while Umādevī is the source of all existence.
Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, Aparājitā,
Bhadrakālī, Mahākālī, and the Yoginī Sthūlakālī;
Indrī, Candrī, Ghorī, Duṣṭī, Lambakī, and Tridaśeśvarī.
The yoginīs dwelling in the villages— Kambojī, Dīpinī, and Cūṣiṇī—
are of terrible form, of great form, with the form of fangs, and formidable;
they wear garlands of skulls, carry khaṭvāṅgas, and possess great supernatural power.
She who holds a sword and a spear in her hands, as well as a vajra, a bow, and so forth—
the five Ḍākinīs of great reality, who accomplish all activities;
the Great Queen of the Yoga Maṇḍala, Vajreśvarī, the Sovereign.
O Vajreśvarī, by this command of the Tathāgata’s great body, which is the emanation of the stainless yoga, I invoke all the various [deities] here. Oṃ kakka kaḍhḍhaṇa bandha bandhana khakkha khādana.
HŪṂ 3 PHAṬ 3 SVĀHĀ. With the *āvāhana* mudrā, [one invokes] Śvetārocanā and Śṛṅkhalā.
This is the mantra for the *saṃtoṣaṇa* mudrā.
Having performed the praise, one should ring the bell:
"O Primordial Supreme Being, O Great Passion, O Great Rapture!
O Samantabhadra, the Soul of All, O Lord of the Vajra-Arrogance, O Lord!"
O supreme being of mind, foremost in meditative concentration, great power of the vajra and vajra-holder;
foremost in the conduct of Samantabhadra, crusher of Māras and the forces of Māra!

O Great Wrath of all wrath, born from the foremost of Buddhas; O Vajra-hūṃkāra, you who utter hūṃ, the bestower of the jewel of Lokeśvara; O Great Passion, Great Bliss, the great wealth of desire and liberation!

O you who are the three worlds, the three states of existence, the three peaks, and the foremost of the three worlds; O you who encompass the triple realm; O you who are the most excellent among the immobile, the unmanifest, the extremely subtle, and the gross collection;
O you who have attained preeminence among the mobile, and who purify the cycle of worldly existence!
O you who are without beginning or end, whose beginning and conclusion are lovely, who are established before all things;
O Great Festival of Reality, the essence of the commitment of the yoga of the heart-seal!
Vajra-wrath, great wrath, you who bind with the flame of universal destruction;
supreme subduer of the most wicked, O Rudra, fierce one, inspirer of fear;
Tathāgata of great accomplishment, great boon of the activity of Dharma.
The path of virtuous action in accordance with the Dharma, which awakens the mind of enlightenment.
The great lotus of universal purity, the great wealth of wisdom and skillful means,
the supreme samādhi of the purification of passion, the Great Lord of universal passion.
O Infinite Space, O Eternal One, Great Abode of all beings,
Manifestation, Glorious Lord, O King, Fulfiler of all hopes!
"Homage be to you! Homage be to you! Homage be to you! Homage again and again!
With devotion I take refuge in you; O Vajrasattva, grant me success today!
Thus one should offer this hymn of praise.

Having worshipped again with flowers and other offerings, and having prostrated, one should offer the *argha* water. One should then request one's desired aim, saying: "O Blessed One, you should forgive whatever deficiency has occurred in my ritual performance."
The welfare of all sentient beings has been accomplished for you; having granted the success that accords with your needs, go now to the realm of the Buddhas, so as to return once more.
One should dismiss the external deity with three snaps of the fingers, using this sequence:
*oṃ gaccha 2 hūṃ svāhā*. Then, having drawn back the emanated circle of deities by means of the breath and caused them to enter one's own body, one should place each deity in its respective location.

Thus, Ghoraḍākinī is on the head; Caṇḍālī in the eyes; Vettālī in the ears and nose; Vajrī on the tongue; Siṃhī, Vyāghrī, Jambukī, and Ulūkī are on the neck, the base of the arms, the heart, and the navel, respectively. The four female gatekeepers are on the right and left thighs and shanks, respectively.
One should cause Pokkasī and the others—whose bindus are directed upward—to enter the tips of the tongues of Pokkasī and the others.
One should cause Ghorā and the others to enter the broad [space] of all five limbs;
having established the vajra-position, one should cause Ugrā and the others to enter;
and one should settle Kapālī and the others upon the row of teeth and the tongue.
One should likewise empower the entire body with these very [deities], such as Amṛtakānti and the rest.
Having stationed the eight worldly deities, beginning with Hari and Brahmā, in the hair-pores and feet respectively,
one should cause the sixteen Bodhisattvas, beginning with Karaṅkabhairava, to enter the luminous rays of the breath of Yogāmbara.

Lāsyā is in the heart; Gandhā between the breasts; Vīṇā in the throat; Puṣpā on the head; Gītā on the two rows of teeth; Dhūpā in the secret place; Nṛtyā on the two arms; Dīpā in the eyes—or else, by way of their forms or by way of their nature as syllables—one should contemplate them. Then, maintaining the ego-identity, "I am Yogāmbara, whose nature is all things," and having performed the protective placement, the empowerment, and the armor, one should preside over the enclosures, the maṇḍalas, and so forth. Whether sleeping, sitting, walking, or even standing—
One should always practice the yoga of the deity with a well-composed mind.
To this extent, it is called excessive practice (atiyoga).
Having fully worshipped the circle of the pledge-maṇḍala with pledge-substances according to the extent of one’s wealth, one should partake of the food in this sequence:

having kindled it with the syllable *kṣūṃ*, purified it with the syllable *yuṃ*, made it solid with the syllable *hūṃ*, and again rendered it into nectar with the syllable *suṃ*; then, having made it of one flavor with the syllable *hūṃ*, placed it in a lotus vessel, and held it in the hand of the sun, one should apply the syllables of nectar. With the thumb and ring finger in the form of the moon, the earth and Mount Meru are visualized.

With the seed-syllables *oṃ ha ho hrīḥ*, which consist of the nature of body, speech, and mind, and possess color, fragrance, and potency, one should place the circles of the individual maṇḍala deities—each having the nature of being free from subject and object—into the apertures and limbs. Having worshipped and prostrated with this, one should satisfy the circle of deities residing within one's own body as desired.

Likewise, in the procedure for the *gaṇamaṇḍala*, one should worship the *gaṇamaṇḍala* established through the yoga of one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) according to the three yogas. Having performed this, one should place a drop (*bindu*) on the forehead, the crown of the head, and the tip of the tongue, and thereafter proceed as one pleases.

Having thus worshipped all the Tathāgatas with offerings of objects according to one's preference, at the conclusion, once again as before, one should worship them with flowers and so forth and then dismiss them.
Afterwards, having offered the discarded bali-offering, one should recite the verse and dismiss them.
This is the verse:

Oṃ kuru 2 vattali mahāvattali siddhimukhi śmaśānavāsini pretamukhi caṇḍakarāli rudhirapriye samayarakṣitayogāmbari kili 2 rāve pitṛvanamadhye bhuñjaha bhakṣaha sahagaṇabhūte dhūmāṅgāri caṇḍakarāli tiṣṭha svīkuru hūṃ gṛhṇa 2 sarvaduṣṭān bhaṃkṣa 2 phreṃ phruṃ pheṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Having formed two vajra-fists, one should raise the white *arocana* [thumb]. One should bend the tips of the two [index fingers] and encircle them at the sides of the mouth.
The mudrā and mantra of the charcoal from the smoke of the offered oblation.
The *Yogāmbarasādhanopāyikā* is completed.
By whatever merit has been acquired through the diligent effort of composing this manual for those striving for the welfare of both self and others, may the world become the glorious Yogāmbara.
It was composed by Amitavajra.
Of those phenomena that arise from causes, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.

This is the religious gift of the Śākya bhikṣu Viśuddhiśrījñāna, a follower of the eminent Mahāyāna and a mendicant who lives on alms; whatever merit is herein, may it, preceded by his teachers, preceptors, mother, and father, be for the attainment of the fruit of unsurpassed knowledge by the entire multitude of sentient beings.
In the increasing reign of auspicious victory of the supreme lord, supreme sovereign, supreme follower of the Sugata, the illustrious Vigrahapāladeva; in the year 13, on the 23rd day of Vaiśākha.
The index finger of the right hand is Śvetā; the middle finger is Dhūmā; the ring finger is Śaṅkhā; the little finger is Padmā; and the thumb is Jñānā.
Likewise for the left hand: Rocanā, Trimalā, Bhaṅgā, Bhūcchattrā, and those designated as Vijñāna.
Oṃ, homage to the glorious Cakrasaṃvara! Oṃ, homage to you whose form is pure; homage to you, the savior from existence! Homage be to you—three times—homage, homage!
With devotion I bow to you; homage be to you, O Gaṇacakra!

Oṃ! Homage to you, O supreme Victor, Cakrasaṃvara, leader of the wheel! Homage to you, Ḍākinī, Lāmikā, and likewise Lamā; homage to you, Rupinī and Khaṇḍarohā! [Homage] to the host of heroes and heroines of the three wheels, to Kākānanā and the others, and to the protectors of the assembly, O Lord of Heroes!
